subject: Accounting
title: Cash vs. Accrual Bookkeeping
description: A short lesson to help you apply Cash vs. Accrual Bookkeeping.

hook.text: You deliver a product in March but get paid in May. When do you record the sale?

buildup.text: Cash bookkeeping records transactions when money changes hands—simple and straightforward.

discovery.text: Accrual bookkeeping records when the transaction occurs—regardless of when cash moves.

twist.text: Cash basis can hide the truth: a profitable business might look broke while waiting for payments.

climax.text: Most small businesses start with cash basis. Growing ones switch to accrual for a clearer picture.

punchline.text: Cash follows the money. Accrual follows the event.

quiz.question: When does accrual bookkeeping record a sale?
options: When the transaction occurs, regardless of payment
At the end of the month

details.summary: Cash and accrual are the two fundamental bookkeeping methods. Cash basis records transactions when money changes hands; accrual basis records them when they're earned or incurred. This topic explains the differences and when each method makes sense.
details.whyItMatters: The choice between cash and accrual profoundly affects reported profits, tax timing, and business decision-making. Using the wrong method can mislead you about your company's true financial position.
takeaways: Cash basis is simpler—record income when received and expenses when paid
Accrual basis matches revenue and expenses to the period they belong to, regardless of cash flow
GAAP requires accrual accounting for most businesses above a certain revenue threshold

faq.question: What is the difference between cash and accrual bookkeeping?
faq.answer: Cash basis records revenue when cash is received and expenses when cash is paid. Accrual basis records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of when money actually changes hands. Accrual gives a more accurate picture of financial health.

faq.question: Which accounting method should a small business use?
faq.answer: Very small businesses and sole proprietors often prefer cash basis for its simplicity. However, businesses with inventory, those exceeding IRS gross receipts thresholds, or those seeking loans or investors typically need accrual basis for accurate reporting.
